title: CARS skills
html:
How to use this sheet: you do not need any background to read it. Start with Key Terms. Each concept then goes: plain English → analogy → 3 core points → for every formula: what it says, when to use it, what each letter means, an everyday example, a step-by-step MCAT example and the trap → where to practice. Read top to bottom once, then use the formulas as a reference.

Covers the user's IDs 8A (CARS foundations), 8B (Reasoning Within Text) and 8C (Reasoning Beyond Text). AAMC tests CARS by these three skills, not by content categories. By AAMC's published breakdown, Foundations of Comprehension is about 30% of CARS questions, Reasoning Within the Text about 30%, and Reasoning Beyond the Text about 40%; passages are split about 50% humanities and 50% social sciences.

Key terms (read first)

TermPlain meaning
MCATThe Medical College Admission Test: a standardized exam with four sections taken by people applying to medical school.
CARSCritical Analysis and Reasoning Skills: the MCAT section made of reading passages and multiple-choice questions about them.
PassageA short piece of writing, typically 500–600 words, followed by several questions (usually 5–7). No outside knowledge is needed.
HumanitiesSubjects about human culture and ideas: art, architecture, dance, ethics, literature, music, philosophy, popular culture, religion, theater.
Social sciencesSubjects that study how people and societies behave: anthropology, archaeology, economics, education, geography, history, linguistics, political science, population health, psychology, sociology.
Paragraph roleThe job a paragraph does in the passage: gives background, states a view, gives an example, raises an objection, answers it.
ArgumentA set of statements where some (the reasons) are offered to convince you of another (the conclusion).
ClaimA statement the author wants you to accept.
EvidenceExamples, data, quotations or reasoning offered to support a claim.
ConclusionThe claim an argument is trying to prove.
Thesis (main idea)The single central claim of the whole passage.
Author's purposeWhy the author wrote the passage: to argue, explain, describe, criticize, compare or defend.
ToneThe author's attitude toward the topic (approving, skeptical, mixed, critical), shown by word choice.
QualifierA word that softens or limits a claim: "often," "may," "I would suggest," "in some cases."
AssumptionAn unstated idea that must be true for the argument to work.
Negation testFlip a possible assumption into its opposite; if the argument then falls apart, the assumption was necessary.
Inference / implicationSomething the passage does not say directly but strongly suggests.
VoiceWhose view a sentence expresses: the author's, or a view the author reports (critics, scholars, "some argue").
Pivot wordA word that signals a turn in the argument: however, yet, but, although, nevertheless.
Strengthen / weakenMake an argument's conclusion more or less likely to be true.
PrincipleThe general rule or reasoning behind the author's view, which can be applied to new cases.
Analogy questionA question asking which new situation follows the same principle as the passage.
DistractorA wrong answer choice designed to look attractive.
ScopeThe range of what the passage actually discusses; "out of scope" = beyond it.
Raw scoreThe number of questions you answer correctly (later converted to a scaled score of 118–132 for CARS).
ProbabilityThe chance something happens, from 0 (never) to 1 (always); 0.25 = 25% = 1 in 4.
Expected numberNumber of tries × probability of success on each: the average you would get over many attempts.

A) CORE CONCEPTS

Concept 1: The CARS section, its three skills and pacing

In plain English: CARS gives you 90 minutes to answer 53 questions about short passages from the humanities and social sciences. You do not need to know anything about the topics; everything you need is in the passage. Doing well depends on a steady pace and knowing which of three skills each question tests.

Analogy: CARS is a 90-minute timed museum tour with 9 rooms. You cannot linger in one room and still see all nine; the budget is about 10 minutes per room.

Official definition: AAMC's CARS section has 53 passage-based questions in 90 minutes. Passages (typically 500–600 words) come about half from the humanities and half from the social sciences, and questions test three skills: Foundations of Comprehension (~30%), Reasoning Within the Text (~30%) and Reasoning Beyond the Text (~40%). No specific outside knowledge or coursework is required.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Format: 53 questions, 90 minutes, passages from humanities (art, philosophy, literature, music, religion, ethics) and social sciences (history, anthropology, economics, political science, population health). Test-takers and prep companies consistently report 9 passages per test (AAMC itself states the question count, not the passage count). Everything must be supported by the passage.
  • Pacing: about 10 minutes per passage (3–4 reading, 6–7 for questions). Skip and return rather than stall on one item; every question is worth the same.
  • Practice volume beats tricks: review every wrong answer by naming its trap type (extreme, out of scope, opposite, irrelevant, distorted) and the skill it tested.
time per passage = 90 min / 9 passages = 10 mintime per question = 90 min / 53 ≈ 1.7 min

In plain words: split the total time evenly across the passages to get a per-passage budget; split it across the questions to get the average time each question can take.

When to use it: before a test, to set checkpoints on the clock; during a practice section, to see whether you are ahead or behind and how much time to make up per remaining passage. When it does not apply: it is an average budget, not a rule for every passage. Harder or longer passages may need 12 minutes and easier ones 8. The per-question figure includes no reading time, so in practice each question gets closer to 1 minute after a 3–4 minute read.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
90 minTotal section timeminutesFixed
9 passagesNumber of passagespassagesEach needs its own read
53Number of questionsquestionsAbout 6 per passage
10 minTime budget per passage, reading includedmin/passageYour checkpoint clock
≈ 1.7 minAverage time per question if reading were freemin/question≈ 1 min 42 s

Everyday example: You have 45 minutes to cook dinner with 5 dishes. That is 45/5 = 9 minutes per dish. If the soup takes 15 minutes, you have to save 6 minutes across the other four dishes, or dessert will not happen.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. Budget: 90/9 = 10 min per passage, so after passage 3 the clock should show 90 − 30 = 60 min left; after passage 6, 30 min.
  2. You check after passage 3 and see only 52 min left: you are 60 − 52 = 8 min behind.
  3. Spread the catch-up over the 6 passages left: 8/6 ≈ 1.3 min to save per passage (shorter reads, flag hard questions).

MCAT trap: Spending 4 minutes on one hard question. That time costs 2–3 easier questions later; flag, guess, move on, come back.

expected questions per skill ≈ skill share × 53

In plain words: multiply each skill's percentage by the total number of questions to estimate how many questions on a test use that skill.

When to use it: to plan study time (put the most practice where the most questions are) or to see how much a weak skill costs you. When it does not apply: AAMC's percentages are approximate, so a given test form will not match them exactly, and individual questions can draw on more than one skill.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
skill shareAAMC's approximate share of questions for a skillfraction0.30 Foundations, 0.30 Within, 0.40 Beyond
53Total CARS questionsquestionsFixed
expected questionsApproximate number testing that skillquestionsWhere your practice time should go

Everyday example: A café knows that about 40% of its 20 daily lunch orders are salads. It should prep about 0.40 × 20 = 8 salads, not exactly 8 every day, but close enough to plan the shopping.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. Foundations ≈ 0.30 × 53 = 15.9 ≈ 16 questions.
  2. Within the Text ≈ 0.30 × 53 ≈ 16; Beyond the Text ≈ 0.40 × 53 = 21.2 ≈ 21.
  3. If you miss half of your Beyond questions (about 10) but only 2 Foundations questions, Beyond is costing you about 10 raw points: practice it first.

MCAT trap: Assuming the split is exact on every form. The percentages are approximate; aim to be strong in all three.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (Instruments That Argue: all three skills), (The Bedside and the Ledger), (The Eloquence of Blank Space), (The Unfair Persuader), (Legible Hands); the bank holds 100 passages, xp001–xp100.

Concept 2: Foundations of Comprehension

In plain English: These questions check that you understood what the passage says: its main point, why it was written, how the author feels, what a word means in that spot, and what a paragraph is doing. The answer is usually found in or near a specific sentence.

Analogy: Foundations questions check that you read the map correctly before you plan a route: where is the author standing, which way is the author facing, and what does each landmark (paragraph) mark?

Official definition: Foundations of Comprehension questions test understanding of the passage's basic components, mainly by inferring meaning or intent from the nearby sentence context: the main idea and purpose, the author's tone, the meaning of words and phrases in context, the role of a paragraph, and what the author implies without stating.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Main idea and purpose: match your one-line thesis; the right answer is neither too narrow (one paragraph's detail) nor too broad (beyond the passage). Purpose verbs matter: "describe" vs. "argue" vs. "defend" vs. "criticize."
  • Tone: read the author's adjectives and qualifiers ("triumphal," "regrettably," "I would suggest"); CARS authors are usually moderate, so extreme tones ("contemptuous," "ecstatic") are rarely right.
  • In-context meaning: reread the full sentence around the word; the answer is the meaning the author uses here, often not the dictionary's first meaning. Implications must follow closely from stated lines.

Everyday example: A friend texts, "Great, the train is late again." The word "great" here means the opposite of its dictionary meaning; you know from the context (and the "again") that the tone is annoyed. Foundations questions ask you to read words the same way, from the surrounding sentence.

Worked example (step by step): The practice passage in Section C.

  1. Paragraph roles (one per sentence group): old ideal of seamless restoration → conservators reject it → visible retouching described → critics object → author answers the objection and states a view.
  2. Thesis: "Visible repair is more truthful than seamless repair." Purpose verb: defend. Tone: measured approval ("I would suggest").
  3. Q1's answer (B, "defend visible retouching as more honest") matches all three, so it is the primary purpose.

MCAT trap: Choosing a "main idea" that is true but covers only one paragraph (too narrow) or the whole field of art history (too broad).

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (main idea), (primary purpose), (central claim), (author's position), (attitude toward instruction), (term as used: kairos), (meaning of "a cloud of variants"), (final phrase).

Concept 3: Reasoning Within the Text

In plain English: These questions ask how the parts of the passage fit together: which reasons support which claims, what the author takes for granted without saying, why a particular example is there, and whose opinion a sentence expresses.

Analogy: Within-the-Text questions ask you to inspect the scaffolding of the building: which beams (evidence) hold up which floors (claims), which beams are hidden in the walls (assumptions), and which one would collapse the floor if removed.

Official definition: Reasoning Within the Text questions ask you to integrate separate parts of the passage into a larger interpretation and to evaluate its arguments: whether claims are supported by evidence, what an argument assumes, how an example or comparison functions, and which views belong to the author vs. other voices.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Claim → evidence: for each claim, find the specific lines that support it; some claims are asserted without support, and the MCAT asks you to tell which.
  • Assumptions: an unstated premise needed for the conclusion. Negation test: if denying the choice destroys the argument, it is a necessary assumption.
  • Function questions ("the author mentions X in order to…"): ask what job the example does for the nearby claim (illustrate, concede, contrast, counter). Separate the author's voice from reported voices; authors often describe a view in order to reject it.

Everyday example: A friend says, "Let's take the highway; it's faster." The unstated assumption is "there is no traffic jam on the highway right now." Negate it ("there is a jam") and the argument collapses, so that assumption was necessary.

Worked example (step by step, negation test): The critics argue "visible marks distract from the image, so retouching should be seamless."

  1. Candidate assumption: "A viewer's immediate impression should take priority."
  2. Negate it: "A viewer's immediate impression should not take priority."
  3. Now the distraction no longer justifies seamless repair, so the argument collapses → it is a necessary assumption (Section C, Q2).

MCAT trap: Confusing the author's voice with a view the author reports. An author may spend a paragraph describing a theory before rejecting it. Check whose view each sentence expresses.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (necessary assumption), (assumption behind reversible restoration), (evidence for a claim), (function of "pester power"), (function of an example), (function of a concession), (purpose of examples).

Concept 4: Reasoning Beyond the Text

In plain English: These questions take the author's idea and test it on something new: a different situation the idea should fit, or a new fact that would make the argument stronger or weaker. They are the largest share of CARS (about 40%).

Analogy: Beyond-the-Text questions take the passage's rule out of the museum and into the street: will the rule still work on a new case, and what new fact would break it?

Official definition: Reasoning Beyond the Text questions ask you to apply or extrapolate the passage's ideas to new situations and to judge how new information would affect the passage's claims (strengthen, weaken, or require revising them).

Core idea (3 points):

  • Apply: first state the passage's principle in one line, then pick the new case that fits the principle, not the surface topic (a repaired vase can match a principle about painting).
  • Strengthen/weaken: identify the exact claim the question targets, then pick the choice that most directly hits the link between that claim and its evidence. A choice about a related but different claim is a distractor.
  • "The author would most likely agree/disagree": predict from the author's stated values and tone; the right answer often extends the author's logic one small step.

Everyday example: A friend's rule for restaurants is "only go where locals eat." Would she like a food truck parked outside a factory at lunch, full of workers? Yes: no dining room, different food, same principle. Would she like a fancy place full of tour buses? No, even though it is "a restaurant."

Worked example (step by step): Principle of the practice passage: "Repairs should be honest: blend from afar, readable up close."

  1. (A) Digitally hiding cracks without comment → dishonest → no. (B) Undetectable marble arm → hidden repair → no.
  2. (C) Lighter clay visible on close inspection → honest and blends from afar → yes.
  3. (D) Refuse to display damaged works → contradicts "damaged and survived" → no. So C (Section C, Q3).

MCAT trap: Choosing the answer about the same topic instead of the same principle. The topic can change; the logic must match.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (analogous situation, strengthening finding), (weaken and analogy), (finding that would challenge), (discovery that would weaken), (analogy for film technique), (practice fitting the proposal), (design the author would praise), (new finding that would weaken).

Concept 5: Passage mapping and tracking voices

In plain English: While reading, jot (or mentally note) one short line per paragraph saying what that paragraph does, plus the author's overall point and tone. This map lets you find the right lines quickly instead of rereading everything, and helps you keep the author's opinion separate from opinions the author is only reporting.

Analogy: A passage map is the table of contents you write yourself: one line per paragraph telling you what job that paragraph does, so you can find evidence fast instead of rereading everything.

Official definition: Passage mapping is the active-reading strategy of summarizing each paragraph's role in the argument, identifying the thesis and tone, and tracking which views belong to the author and which to others.

Core idea (3 points):

  • One note per paragraph: its job ("old view," "author rejects," "example," "concession," "author's answer"), then a one-line thesis plus the author's tone.
  • Watch signal words: pivot words (however, yet, but), emphasis words (crucially, above all) and opinion markers (I argue, it seems, I would suggest) mark where the author's own view lives.
  • Track voices: "many conservators," "critics," "some historians" are not the author until the author endorses them.

Everyday example: Watching a courtroom drama, you keep track of who is speaking: the prosecutor, the defense lawyer, a witness, the judge. If you mixed up the prosecutor's accusation with the judge's ruling, you would get the ending wrong. Passage voices work the same way.

Worked example (step by step): Map the Section C passage in 5 notes.

  1. P1 "old ideal: seamless" → P2 "conservators: hiding = replacing past with guess" → P3 "visible retouching = damaged and survived."
  2. P4 "critics: distracting, modern taste" → P5 "Yet objection assumes first impression > knowledge; author: honest repair is more truthful."
  3. The pivot "Yet" and the marker "I would suggest" locate the author's own view in the last two sentences.

MCAT trap: Reading for details and memorizing facts. CARS rewards knowing the structure and the author's stance; details can be looked up.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (attitude toward scholars), (attitude toward the sociological analysis), (attitude toward the "triumphal" account), (role of a contrast), (function of the final paragraph), (paragraph function).

Concept 6: Answer elimination

In plain English: When the right answer is not obvious, cross out the wrong ones. Wrong CARS answers fall into a few repeating types, and each one you remove raises your chance of being right. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a question blank.

Analogy: Eliminating answers is a police lineup: you may not recognize the culprit at once, but you can usually rule out the suspects who were somewhere else that night.

Official definition: Answer elimination is the systematic removal of choices that are unsupported by the passage, using recurring distractor types, so that the remaining choice is the one best supported by specific lines.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Five common distractor types: too extreme ("always," "never," "proves," "only"), out of scope (not discussed), opposite (reverses the author's view), true but irrelevant (accurate but does not answer this question), distorted (mixes passage words with a wrong relationship).
  • Real-world truth is a trap: CARS rewards what the passage supports; a factually correct but unsupported or irrelevant choice is wrong.
  • Predict first, then eliminate: say the answer in your own words before reading the choices, then remove choices by type and confirm the survivor against specific lines.
P(correct guess) = 1 / (4 − number of choices eliminated)

In plain words: if you must guess, your chance of being right is one divided by the number of choices you have not ruled out.

When to use it: deciding whether to spend 30 more seconds eliminating one more choice, or estimating how many points careful elimination is worth on hard questions. When it does not apply: it assumes you guess at random among the remaining choices and that every choice you eliminated really was wrong. If you wrongly eliminate the correct answer, your chance drops to 0.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
4Answer choices per questionchoicesA–D
number eliminatedChoices you ruled out with confidencechoices0–3
P(correct guess)Chance of being right if you guess among the restprobability25% → 33% → 50% → 100%

Everyday example: A street game hides a ball under one of 4 cups. Guessing blind wins 1/4 = 25% of the time. If you saw that two of the cups were empty, you choose between 2 and win 1/2 = 50% of the time.

MCAT worked example (step by step): On 8 hard questions you can eliminate 2 choices each.

  1. Chance per question: 1/(4 − 2) = 1/2.
  2. Expected correct = 8 × 1/2 = 4, versus 8 × 1/4 = 2 by blind guessing.
  3. Two confident eliminations double your expected score on those items.

MCAT trap: Eliminating the right answer because it sounds modest. The correct CARS answer is often the cautious, qualified one; the extreme one is the distractor.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (author would DISAGREE), (statement the author would accept), (whom the author would criticize), (implication of the final sentence), (author's attitude toward harm-based arguments).

Pathway: answering any CARS question (original 520 Quest diagram)

C) 3 MCAT-STYLE PRACTICE QUESTIONS

Practice passage (original, written for 520 Quest):

Museums once treated restoration as a return to an object's "original" state, filling gaps so seamlessly that visitors could not tell new paint from old. Many conservators now reject that ideal. A restoration that hides itself, they argue, quietly replaces the past with the restorer's guess about it. The newer practice of visible retouching—hatching in a missing area with fine lines that blend at a distance but separate up close—asks viewers to accept a work as damaged and survived rather than whole. Critics reply that such marks distract from the image and impose a modern scholarly taste on works made for devotion or delight. Yet this objection assumes that the viewer's first impression matters more than the viewer's knowledge of what is actually there. An honest repair, I would suggest, is not a lesser kind of beauty but a different and more truthful one.

Q1 (Foundations). The author's primary purpose is to:

  • A) describe the history of museum restoration techniques
  • B) defend visible retouching as more honest than seamless restoration
  • C) argue that damaged artworks should not be restored at all
  • D) show that critics of visible retouching misunderstand devotional art

Answer: B. The final sentence states the author's view: honest, visible repair is "more truthful."

  • A is wrong: the history is background for an argument, not the purpose.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: too extreme; the author favors a kind of restoration, not none.
  • D is wrong: the author answers the critics' assumption about first impressions, not their understanding of devotional art.

Q2 (Within the Text). The critics' objection, as the author presents it, depends on which assumption?

  • A) Visible retouching damages the original paint
  • B) A viewer's immediate visual experience should take priority
  • C) Conservators should not have scholarly training
  • D) Seamless restoration is cheaper

Answer: B. The author says the objection "assumes that the viewer's first impression matters more than the viewer's knowledge."

  • A is wrong: the passage never claims physical damage.
  • B is correct.
  • C is wrong: "scholarly taste" is mentioned, but nothing about training.
  • D is wrong: cost is never discussed.

Q3 (Beyond the Text). Which new practice would the author most likely approve of?

  • A) Digitally removing cracks from a photograph of a fresco before printing it in a guidebook, without comment
  • B) Rebuilding a missing statue arm in a matching marble so the repair cannot be detected
  • C) Displaying a repaired vase with its new sections in a slightly lighter clay that is visible on close inspection
  • D) Refusing to display any damaged objects

Answer: C. It parallels visible retouching: it blends from afar but is honest up close.

  • A is wrong: it hides damage, which the author calls replacing the past with a guess.
  • B is wrong: undetectable repair is the ideal the author rejects.
  • C is correct.
  • D is wrong: the author values showing works as "damaged and survived."

More in the 5,180 Qbank: Full CARS passages with 5–6 questions each, for example passage "Legible Hands" (visible retouching), "Instruments That Argue", "The Instructed Child" and "The Unfair Persuader" (100 passages, xp001–xp100).
